'''Watt Wetmore Webb''' (August 27, 1927 – October 29, 2020)<ref name="cornell"/> was an American biophysicist, known for his co-invention (with [[Winfried Denk]] and [[Jim Strickler]]) of [[Two-photon excitation microscopy|multiphoton microscopy]] in 1990.<ref><div class="csl-entry">Denk, W., Strickler, J. H., Webb, W. W. (1990). Two-photon laser scanning fluorescence microscopy. ''Science'', ''248''(4951). https://doi.org/10.1126/science.2321027</div></ref><ref>So, P.T.C., Kim, K.H., Buehler, C., Masters, B.R., Hsu, L., Dong, CY. (2001). Basic Principles of Multiphoton Excitation Microscopy. In: Periasamy, A. (eds) Methods in Cellular Imaging. Methods in Physiology. Springer, New York, NY. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-7513-2_9</ref>

== Early life and education==
Watt Wetmore Webb was born on August 27, 1927, in [[Kansas City, Missouri]].<ref name=ElsonObit>{{cite journal |vauthors=Elson E |title=Watt W. Webb: His measurements of the seemingly inaccessible broadened the horizons of biophysics |journal=Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A |volume=118 |issue=12 |pages= |date=March 2021 |pmid=33692168 |pmc=7999940 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2101879118|bibcode=2021PNAS..11801879E |doi-access=free }}</ref> Webb hailed from a family of bankers. In 1891, his grandfather, Watt Webb, had founded the [[Missouri Savings Bank]], an organization that would be led by Webb's uncle Wilson S. Webb, and eventually his father Watt Webb Jr.<ref name=KCTimes>{{cite news|title=Watt Webb Jr. Dies |work=Kansas City Times |date=9 January 1960 |via=NewsPaper Archive |url=https://newspaperarchive.com/us/missouri/kansas-city/kansas-city-times/1960/01-09/page-6/ |page=6}}</ref> Due to a long illness, Watt W. Webb did not start formal schooling until the age of 10.<ref name=BonettaInt>{{cite journal|title=Profile of Watt W. Webb, D. Sc. |journal=BioTechniques |volume=38 |issue=4 |author=Bonetta L |date=30 May 2018 |page=515 |doi=10.2144/05384SP01|pmid=15884665 |doi-access=free }}</ref> As a young man, Webb worked at the family banking business; when Webb joined [[MIT]] as an undergraduate at 16 years old, he acceded to his parents request that he study business administration to prepare him to join the family banking business.<ref name=BonettaInt/><ref name=ElsonObit/> Despite his business major, Webb took a number of science and engineering courses, and raced sailboats as part of MIT's sailing team.<ref name=BonettaInt/> He completed his bachelor's degree in business and engineering administration in 1947, then went to work as an industrial engineer at [[Union Carbide|Union Carbide Research Labs]] in [[Niagara Falls, New York]], focused on [[submerged arc welding]].<ref name="cornell"/><ref name=BonettaInt/> He returned to MIT, completing his [[Sc.D.|doctorate]] in materials science physics and mathematics in 1955.<ref name=ElsonObit/>

== Research career ==
After his doctorate, Webb returned to Union Carbide as assistant director of research.<ref name=PistonObit>{{cite journal |vauthors=Piston DW, Elson EL |title=Pioneers in biomedical optics: special section honoring Professor Watt Webb of Cornell University |journal=J Biomed Opt |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=855–912 |date=2004 |pmid=15447005 |doi=10.1117/1.1790004 |bibcode=2004JBO.....9..855P |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=BonettaInt/> In 1961, Watt moved to [[Ithaca, New York]], to join the [[Cornell University]] faculty as an associate professor of engineering physics.<ref name=ZipfelObit>{{cite journal |vauthors=Zipfel W, Xu C, Elson E, Maiti S |title=Memorial Viewpoint for Watt W. Webb: An Experimentalist's Experimentalist |journal=J Phys Chem B |volume=125 |issue=11 |pages=2793–2795 |date=March 2021 |pmid=33622036 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.1c01045 |s2cid=232037668 |url=}}</ref> There, in the early 1960s he developed the first stable [[superconducting magnet]] along with then-undergraduate [[Malcolm Beasley]] (who went on to do his [[PhD thesis]] work in Watt's lab as well).<ref name="cornell"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/47101 |accessdate=19 November 2022 |title=Malcom Beasley - Interview by David Zierler |date=5 February 2021 |publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> Webb was promoted to full professor in 1965.<ref name=ZipfelObit/>

In the early 1970s, Webb collaborated with Elliot Elson to develop a method to monitor the kinetics of chemical reactions, focused particularly on the binding of [[ethidium bromide]] to [[DNA]]. The result was the development of [[fluorescence correlation spectroscopy]], which they described in a series of papers from 1972 to 1974.<ref name=ElsonObit/>{{efn|The papers, as cited by Elson in Webb's obituary, are: {{Unbulleted list|{{cite journal|vauthors=Magde D, Elson EL, Webb WW |title=Thermodynamic fluctuations in a reacting system—Measurement by fluorescence correlation spectroscopy |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=29 |pages=705–708 |date=1972|issue=11 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.29.705 |bibcode=1972PhRvL..29..705M }}|{{cite journal|vauthors=Elson E, Magde D |title=Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy I. Conceptual basis and theory |journal=Biopolymers |volume=13 |pages=1–27 |date=1974|doi=10.1002/bip.1974.360130102 |s2cid=97201376 }}|{{cite journal|vauthors=Magde D, Elson EL, Webb WW |title=Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy II. An experimental realization |journal=Biopolymers |volume=13 |pages=29–61 |date=1974|issue=1 |doi=10.1002/bip.1974.360130103 |pmid=4818131 |s2cid=2832069 }}}}}}

From 1983–1988 Webb served as director of the college's School of Applied and Engineering Physics.<ref name="cornell"/> In the late 1980s, Webb – along with then PhD student in his laboratory [[Winfried Denk]] – built the first [[Two-photon excitation microscopy|multiphoton microscope]].<ref name="cornell"/>

In 1998, Watt was named to an [[endowed professorship]], the S. B. Eckert Professor in Engineering.<ref name=ZipfelObit/>

He has directed the NIH Developmental Resource for Biophysical Imaging Opto-Electronics for the last 20 years. He was on the board of directors and executive committee of the Cornell Center for Technology, Enterprise, and Commercialization, was affiliated with the university's Biophysics Program, the Cornell Center for Materials Research, the Nanobiotechnology Center and served on the Executive Committee of the Neuroscience Focus Area. He was a visiting scholar at [[Stanford University]], a [[Guggenheim fellow]], and a scholar in residence at the NIH Fogarty International Center for Advanced Study.

He was a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], a founding fellow of the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]], and an elected member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1993), the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (1995), and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="cornell"/>

He also received several awards for his work, including the American Physical Society's [[Max Delbruck Prize]] (then called the "Biological Physics Prize") in 1991,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/delbruck.cfm |accessdate=20 November 2022 |title=Max Delbruck Prize in Biological Physics |publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref> [[Case Western Reserve University]]'s [[Michelson–Morley Award]] in 1999, the [[Rank Prize for Optoelectronics]] in 2000,<ref name="cornell"/> and the New York Microscopical Society's Ernst Abbe Award in 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nyms.org/past-abbe-awards/ |accessdate=20 November 2022 |title=Past Abbe Awards |publisher=New York Microscopical Society|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053823/http://www.nyms.org/past-abbe-awards/ |archive-date=March 4, 2016 }}</ref>

Watt retired from active research as an [[emeritus professor]] in 2012.<ref name=ZipfelObit/>

He published over 310 papers in solid state and chemical physics and in biological physics; with 22 U.S. patents plus many foreign patents. He was active as a consultant and in various national advisory committees and professional societies.

His doctoral students include [[Malcolm Beasley]], [[Winfried Denk]], [[Neil Gershenfeld]], and [[David W. Tank]].<ref>Physics Tree: [http://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=1212 Watt W Webb Details]</ref>

Webb died on October 29, 2020, in New York City at the age of 93.<ref name="cornell">{{cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2020/11/watt-webb-biological-imaging-techniques-pioneer-dies |title=Watt Webb, biological imaging techniques pioneer, dies|website=Cornell University|access-date=November 6, 2020}}</ref>

== FCS and MPM ==

Professor Webb pioneered the techniques of [[Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy|Fluorescence Correlation Spectroscopy]] (FCS) in 1972<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Magde D, Elson EL, Webb WW |title=Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy. II. An experimental realization |year=1974 |journal=Biopolymers |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=29–61 |doi=10.1002/bip.1974.360130103 |pmid=4818131|s2cid=2832069 }}</ref> and [[Multi-photon microscopy (disambiguation)|Multiphoton microscopy]] (MPM) in 1990.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Denk W, Strickler JH, Webb WW |title=Two-photon laser scanning fluorescence microscopy |year=1990 |journal=Science |volume=248 |issue=4951 |pages=73–76 |pmid=2321027|bibcode = 1990Sci...248...73D |doi = 10.1126/science.2321027 }}</ref> FCS enables single-molecule detection in solutions at nanomolar concentrations and provides temporal resolution of the dynamic processes of individual molecules signaled by their fluorescence. FCS reveals molecular mobility, conformational fluctuations and chemical reactions in solutions and allows the detection of extremely sparse molecules and particles. In situ measurements of the dynamics of fluorescence flicker by FCS, photobleaching, phototoxicity, and induced fluorescence are being used to discern dynamics of biological processes and molecular mechanisms of disease. Multiphoton excitation in laser scanning fluorescence microscopy provides for high resolution, high signal-to-noise imaging in living cells and deep in turbid tissues in vivo and significantly reduces photodamage and minimizes image degradation due to scattering and autofluorescence. His laboratory at Cornell University continues to extend the frontiers of these technologies, now for example extending MPM and FCS to imaging molecular processes within the cellular nucleus for gene expression in vivo. Recently initiated is the development of technology for introduction of MPM into Medical Endoscopy for in vivo, in situ real time diagnostics.

== Honors ==

In 2010 Webb was awarded the [[Alexander Hollaender Award in Biophysics]] by the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|title=Alexander Hollaender Award in Biophysics|url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_hollaender|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060102123544/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_hollaender|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 2, 2006|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|accessdate=February 13, 2011}}</ref> Was awarded the [[Rosenstiel Award]] in 2013.

== Personal life ==
Webb was an avid sailor, together with his wife Page Chapman – whom he met sailing<ref>{{cite web | url=https://starclass.org/classic/artman/publish/printer_516.shtml.html | title=Page Chapman Webb 1928-2010 }}</ref> on the [[Charles River]] while Webb pursued his bachelor's degree.<ref name=PistonObit/><ref name=PageObit>{{cite news|url= https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/theithacajournal/name/page-webb-obituary?pid=145954806 |accessdate=18 November 2022 |title=Page Webb 1928–2010 |work=Ithaca Journal |date=13 October 2010}}</ref> Together they raced sailing yachts across the northeast well into their 70s.<ref name=PageObit/> They had three children together, a son in 1954, and twin boys in 1956.<ref name=PageObit/>
